DisruptionBench and Complimentary New Models: Two Advancements
in Machine Learning Driven Disruption Prediction
Lucas Spangher1 · Matteo Bonotto2 · William Arnold3 · Dhruva Chayapathy4 · Tommaso Gallingani5 ·
Alexander Spangher6 · Francesco Cannarile2 · Daniele Bigoni5 · Eliana de Marchi2 · Cristina Rea1

Abstract
Plasma disruptions remain a major obstacle to sustained commercial operation of tokamak-based fusion devices. Although
machine learning (ML) methods have shown promise for predicting disruptions, their performance and generalizability
suffer from a lack of common benchmarks and comprehensive multi-device evaluations. To address this, we present
DisruptionBench, a new benchmarking platform designed to standardize how ML-driven disruption prediction systems
are trained and evaluated on multi-machine data. DisruptionBench spans three devices - Alcator C-Mod, DIII-D, and EAST
- and includes tasks of varying difficulty: zero-shot, few-shot, and many-shot training regimes to assess each model’s ability
to transfer learned representations to new or data-limited machines. We evaluate four state-of-the-art ML architectures. Two
are re-implementations of notable prior work: a random forest (Cristina Rea in PPCF 60:084008, 2018) and the Hybrid Deep
Learner (HDL) (Zhu in NC 61: 026607, 2020). We also propose two new approaches tailored for disruption prediction: a
transformer-based model inspired by GPT-2, capable of learning long-range temporal dependencies through self-attention,
and a Continuous Convolutional Neural Network (CCNN) that leverages continuous kernels to capture subtle variations in
plasma signals. Across the nine benchmarking tasks, the CCNN demonstrates consistently strong performance and achieves
the highest overall Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC) in intra-machine tests (up to 0.97 on C-Mod). Nevertheless, the
GPT-2-based approach and HDL can outperform CCNN in specific transfer scenarios, particularly when the test machine is
underrepresented in training data. We further analyze the significance of memory length in capturing precursor phenomena,
providing evidence that longer context windows can boost predictive accuracy.

Introduction
Plasma disruptions in nuclear fusion tokamaks1 present
signifificant challenges for both control and predictive mod-
eling. Disruptions are sudden events that lead to a complete
loss of plasma confifinement, posing a serious threat to the
integrity of the reactor due to forces and heat loads on the
tokamak components. Effffective disruption management is
therefore essential for the safe and sustained operation of
plasma reactors, particularly as the design of future devices
like ITER and DEMO depends on achieving high-perfor-
mance, disruption-free operation. Recreating disruptions in
physical simulations is particularly challenging for at least
two reasons. (1) The variety of possible causes (e.g. control
fault, setpoint deviation, human error, tokamak impurities)
are large and many possible causes themselves do not have
accurate simulations [3–5]. (2) Unobserved factors might

[6, 7] and may increase probability of disruption in future
discharges. Thus, physical simulations may be insuffiffifficient
for predicting disruptions [1].
The combination of these factors makes physical
simulations insuffiffifficient for reliably predicting disruptions,
especially under varied operational scenarios [1]. This has
motivated the growing interest in data-driven surrogate
models, which leverage large experimental datasets to
complement and extend traditional physics-based models.
These surrogate models are proving instrumental in
capturing complex, nonlinear relationships within the
data, allowing for more accurate disruption prediction
and avoidance strategies. Their integration into plasma
control systems is critical, as these systems must rapidly
and adaptively respond to changing plasma conditions to
prevent disruptions.
In this work, we lay the groundwork to accelerate our
understanding of disruptions in tokamak plasmas through
ML. In recent years, ML fifields as diverse as natural language
processing (i.e., NLP; see common abbreviations in Table 7
of Appendix B), computer vision (CV), energy systems,
and robotics have seen impressive modeling advancements
[8–16]; less visible have been the comprehensive
benchmarking suites in each field that have laid the
groundwork for these breakthroughs. These benchmarking
suites standardize evaluation approaches for core tasks in
each domain (e.g. object recognition in CV), and allow
diverse capabilities of different models to be validated
against each other. Without such benchmarks, accelerated
progress in these fifields would not have been possible; with
them, not only can the core tasks outlined by the benchmarks
be addressed, but deeper insights and more advanced tasks
become possible. We consider this benchmark for tokamak
plasma disruption prediction a major enabling result of this
paper.
In the current work, we introduce a benchmark aimed at
modeling disruption prediction in tokamak devices. We out-
line 9 tasks, ranging from easy, medium and hard. The tasks
are designed to test how well models can generalize across
different tokamak devices for the scientific purpose of

relying on particularities of each tokamak; such particulari-

single machine, but might block our ability to understand
general physical dynamics. Then, we use this benchmark
to evaluate a wide range of current state-of-the-art models
for disruption prediction. In summary, our contributions in
this work are:
1. Real-time, generalized model benchmarking platform:
We present the fifirst a common benchmarking platform
for disruption prediction across multiple different
tokamaks. Our benchmark mimics how a model would
be used in real-time tokamak operation, incorporating
logic that mimics operational regimes to which a real-
time disruption prediction model would be subjected.
2. Model Comparison: We compare an array of state-of-
the-art models in a fifirst-of-a-kind rigorous benchmarking
exercise. All told, we re-implement DIII-D ’s Random
Forest (RF) [17] and the Hybrid Deep Learner (HDL) [2]
and introduce two new models, a Generative Pretrained
Transformer 2 (which we shall refer to as GPT-2) and
a Continuous Convolutional Neural Network (CCNN).
Our top performing transfer approach achieves an
overall Area Under the Receiving Operating Curve
(AUC) of 0.83 and F2-score of 0.62 (for a defifinition of
the evaluation metrics AUC and F2-score, see [18] and
[19] respectively.) We demonstrate higher gains when
using data only from the test tokamak, with the AUC
rising to a maximum of 0.97 and F2-score to a maximum
of 0.89. While this is still not a stopping point for model
development, especially for those that seek to transfer
training of disruption prediction from existing machines
to new, unseen machines [20], it represents a notable
step forward.
3. Exploratory Insights: The models feature considerable
variation which allow qualitative conclusions drawn;
most notably (1) sample rate dependence: the HDL and
the GPT-2 are sample rate dependent, whereas the RF
and CCNN are not, the implications of which we will
discuss in Sect. 5. (2) Long-term memory: all models
feature limited data context except for the GPT-2, which
we study across difffferent trials, varying in the amount of
data context the model sees. We relate this physically to
the question of whether long term memory is important
in plasmas, which our data supports.
We see greater potential for the present work, beyond the
disruption prediction task directly focused on. As mentioned,
benchmarks in NLP, CV and robotics have solved core tasks

Related Work
Disruption prediction through ML was fifirst explored through
in the 2000’s [21], and a body of literature has ballooned in
recent years [2, 3, 17, 22–31]. Especially noteworthy models
include advanced architectures such as temporal [32, 33] and
spatial [34] convolutional neural nets (CNNs) and variational
autoencoders [35]; others combine spatio-temporal models
such Zhu et al.’s Hybrid Deep Learner (HDL) [2]. Other
models feature tree-like [1, 36, 37], recurrent structure [38],
manifold learning and generative mapping [39], and survival
analysis [40, 41].
Existing ML models of disruption prediction fall short of
robust “production quality” in several ways.
1. Evaluation approaches are not standardized: There
does not exist a commonly used benchmarking platform
for disruption prediction, or agreed-upon evaluation
metric, that mimics real-time disruption prediction
environments. Some papers use an end of discharge
AUC classifification, whereas others use a hysteresis type
evaluation but have not made their code public [2, 42–
44]. Nor does there exist rigorous comparisons between
difffferent model architectures to provide a quantitative
suggestion on the model architecture to develop for a new
tokamak.
2. State-of-the-art systems are not accurate enough for real
world use-cases: Disruption prediction accuracy rates
need improvement. Reported results typically reach 90%
True Positive Rate (TPR) for a 5% False Positive Rate
(FPR) [38]. The TPR and FPR are defifined, respectively,
as the rate at which the model correctly and incorrectly
guesses a positive result, with the potential to engage the
Disruption Mitigation System (DMS). Next generation
devices will require models to reach 95% TPR at a 5%
FPR [45], which means we still need progress.
3. Models are not tested across multiple tokamaks: Most
deployed models, such as DIII-D ’s Random Forest (RF),
contain signifificant historical data from the tokamak
they are deployed on in their training set [43]. This is
easier than training on difffferent tokamaks and testing
on a new tokamak, which may have difffferent machine
characteristics and physical dynamics. However, in
the current state of tokamak production, each tokamak
produced is a unique design and thus zero shot transfer
is a pressing challenge. When considering zero-shot
transfer metrics, state of the art models drop to 77%
TPR at 5% FPR [2].
4. Prior models are dependent on a tokamak’s
unique sampling rate: Most tokamaks today record
measurements of plasma discharges features with
different sampling rates, due to the use of different
diagnostic instruments [46]. Since nearly all state-of-
the-art models we tested were designed only for one
tokamak, they have been trained with difffferent sampling
rates.
This further impedes the transferability of models
across tokamaks, as we will discuss in Sect. 3.
5. The memory within a tokamak plasma is poorly
understood: It is unclear how long the physical
“memory” of a plasma is relevant to an ML model – i.e.
the time window between which one plasma state may
affffect a future state. The physical dynamics of plasma
are affffected on timescales of around 200 milliseconds
(temperature profiles can vary on sawtooth period
timescales, and magnetohydrodynamics can evolve on
Alfvenic or resistive wall timescales, both less than 200
ms) [2, 43, 47]. However, real-time tokamak operation
may be affffected by other factors that have long time-
delayed effects and may be important for models to
consider. Consider, for instance, a case in which the inner
wall has impurities deposited from a prior discharge.
Trace impurities may impact the ramp-up dynamics
when they easily break free, and then a larger impurity
injection may occur seconds into the discharge, causing
disruption. In this case complex models may fifind it useful
to remember dynamics at the start of the discharge. So,
how much data context should we explicitly show our
models when asking them to make decisions about a
plasma state seconds away from its start? We fifind this
question underaddressed in the literature.
6. Dataset sizes: No prior study of disruption prediction
uses a “big data approach”; that is, none are trained
on database of multiple tokamaks with more than 2
gigabytes (GB) of discharge data, featuring fifine enough
time resolution to suffiffifficiently capture many examples
of each type of disruption. For a further discussion on
the benefifits of big data and the diffiffifficulties in defifining
it, please see ref. [48]. Previously, Rea et al. [1] and

Zhu et al. [2] used the same database of roughly 17k
discharges, Aymerich et al. [44] used 419 discharges
to train the deployed CNN on JET, and Cannas et al.
[42] used just 119 disruptive discharges. Yet modern
NLP only started to shine when internet-scale datasets
were scraped and used [49]. In order to unlock the
expressivity of advanced ML models, much more data
is needed [48, 50].
Open Evaluation Benchmarking Tool
and Included Tasks
Overview
We present DisruptionBench, the first standardized,
general evaluation framework in nuclear fusion research.
DisruptionBench brings together 9 disruption prediction
tasks, with task progression emphasizing assessing models’
abilities to generalize to new tokamaks. It is the first
framework in nuclear fusion to be model agnostic, machine-
agnostic and to model dynamics at a range of different
sampling frequencies.
Our benchmark is public and we encourage the
community to use it for reproducibility. Indeed, if reading
this with collaboration in mind, please feel free to use and
actively distribute our framework, which may be found
publicly at the following GitHub https://github.com/MIT-
PSFC/DisruptionBench.
Each task in DisruptionBench is framed as a time-series
classifification task, where the time-series is k-dimensions,
and each dimension d is a difffferent measurement of the
plasma made by a tokamak’s instrumentation. Given an
input sequence x of length t, and output probabilities y of
the discharge ending in disruption, which changes at each
timestep, p(y x 0 , ...x i ) ∀ i ∈ t, DisruptionBench simulates
the dynamics of a standard tokamak’s DMS trigger. These
are: with a h|igh and low probability threshold, and a
hysteresis value, DisruptionBench intervenes when enough
probability predictions occur consecutively above a high
threshold without dropping below the low threshold. See
implementation details in Sect. 3.3. DisruptionBench is
currently composed of trials from three difffferent tokamaks,
the Alcator C-Mod tokamak hosted by the Massachusetts
Institute of Technology, the DIII-D tokamak hosted by
General Atomics, and the EAST tokamak hosted by the
Chinese Academy of Science. For a longer discussion on
the physical difffferences between the three, see [17]. We will
incorporate data from more tokamaks in future work.
Benchmarking Tasks
Our framework allows for at least 9 difffferent subdomains
of benchmarking tasks. Each task is constructed by
selecting one setting each from the following three sets:
(1) “New Machine”: select 1-of-3 different tokamaks
in the dataset as a “new machine” (we will describe the
meaning of this shortly); (2) Data-Split: select broadly
within 1-of-3 difffferent domains of data composition putting
the “new machine” in training and test sets; and (3) Data
Composition: a more diffffuse category describing selecting
how many disruptions or non disruptions to include in
the training set, and from which machines. The pairwise
combination of three selections from the fifirst set, one of
three selections from the second set, and a user’s broad
choice from the third set yields 9+ general areas of settings.
We describe each set now.
(1)“New Machine”: A key desiderata in our benchmark is
to test how well models trained on an existing set of tokamak
observations can make predictions about a new tokamak. This
is a key measure of a model’s ability to learn fundamental
physical dynamics. The options in this set are each of the
three tokamaks: (i) EAST, (ii) DIII-D and (iii) Alcator
C-Mod. Selecting a tokamak means that the training set will
be composed of all discharges from the other tokamaks, and
the data from the selected tokamak will be distributed across
training and test sets in varying amounts (the exact amounts
are determined by the selection from set # 2, described next).
We describe dynamics of each tokamak now and reported a
list of major tokamak parameters in Table 1.
1. EAST: Certain instabilities in EAST may evolve more
slowly across time compared to DIII-D and Alcator
C-Mod [51]; thus, we expect tasks with EAST as “new
machine” to be an easier set of tasks. EAST’s discharges
last longer than other tokamaks, so we expect tasks with
EAST as “new machine” to favor models focusing on
longer-term trends. The EAST tokamak also routinely
executes discharges in new parts of the operational
domain (e.g. setting the record for internal temperature
in 2018 and discharge lengths in 2021 and 2023 [52]),
so these tasks also test model transfer to new regimes
[53]. Furthermore, the dataset includes periods of time
when plasma facing components of EAST were stainless
steel, and a combination of graphite and tungsten, which
is a wall-choice that is becoming more common in newer
machines. EAST is a superconducting machine, meaning
that it is composed of superconducting magnets [54].
2. DIII-D: DIII-D as a machine is structurally similar
to EAST: it has similar size, magnetic fields, wall
composition and currents. However, it is not a
superconducting machine, and so its pulse lengths tend
to be shorter, and the data is sampled at a fifiner rate.

Therefore, tasks using DIII-D as the new machine may
feature the model’s ability to generalize to up-sampled
data regimes for a similar operational regime [55].
3. Alcator C-Mod: Alcator C-Mod is considered the hardest
machine in our dataset to test on. Its pulse lengths
are short (i.e. between 0 and 2 s), and relative to the
others, around 30% of the disruptions are caused by
impurity injection, which results in fast instabilities on
the order of milliseconds [56]. In our dataset, it is also
sampled most fifinely, meaning that models would have
to generalize to higher sampling regimes.
(2)Data-Split: This setting is designed to test how much
data is needed from a new machine to learn its dynamics.
We design this test to mimic (i) zero-shot, (ii) few-shot
and (iii) many-shot setups in NLP, where pretrained large
langage models (LLMs) start as generalists (i.e. pretrained
on a very large quantity of general purpose data), and
are then steered by difffferent amounts of data into being
specialists. In this setting, each selection determines how
much data from the “new machine” is included in the
training data.
1. Zero-shot tasks: In the zero-shot case, no amount of
data from the “new machine” is included in the training
set, and the models are only trained on data from the
two other tokamaks. This setting simulates the tasks
in which we prepare models for a future device, and
directly tests how the physical dynamics learned from
the other machines transfer to the new machine. The user
may choose their desired proportion of disruptions/non-
disruptions from the existing machines.
2. Few shot tasks: In these cases, small amounts of
data from the “new machine”, which we defifine as 20
examples or fewer, is included in the training set. This
may include datapoints of length from 0 to 20 timesteps,
or it can include entire sets of examples, i.e. a set of non-
disruptions from the new device. These tasks allow the
simulation of models inserted into the early running
stages of a future tokamak. The test set may be sampled
from the remaining unused discharges, but we also
provide test-set lists for convenience.
3. Many shot tasks: The user may simulate tasks in which all
available data from the “new machine” is included in the
training set. These are useful tests for a commercialization
case in which numerous versions of a commercial tokamak
already exist, and the model may be fifit to future iterations.
In the data that we provide, the proportion of disruptive
shots is true to realtime operation of those specifific devices;
thus, this would be the most physically accurate selection.
(3)Training Class Composition: Once a user selects their
new machine and the style of test they desire, the user may
further defifine a data breakdown to compose their training
set. Specififically, this is represented the exact number of
disruptions or non-disruptions to include from the new
machine or existing machines. While this is a broad decision,
we note some decision factors: (a) Including all of the data
may help a model learn the true distribution of classes, which
may be closer to the real-world frequency of disruptions (and
is certainly closer to the test set composition.) However,
models may often become biased towards the majority
class, often predicting "non-disruption" for every example
unless conditioned otherwise. (b) Depending on the model
architecture, a user may be inclined to adopt one training
composition strategy over another. Models like decision
trees, for example, handle imbalance better than others,
which may need the inclusion of self-supervised techniques
like SMOTE.
For examples of which cases are possible to create
from DisruptionBench, please see the six cases we have
constructed for our benchmarking exercise in Table 4. While
Table 4 lists only training set compositions for all cases, a
test set for all cases is fifirst composed by randomly separating

of the multimachine dataset’s size. Once sampled, these test
set compositions were fifixed and recorded for all subsequent
model development and comparison, and are available as
individual fifiles in the repo associated with the GPT-2 (see
Sect. 5.3.) Note that these are not an exhaustive list of the
cases possible to construct from DisruptionBench, but just
the cases we choose to focus on in our analysis.
We acknowledge that some of the predefined cases
available for user selection-such as our few-shot scenario
comprising 20 disruptive discharges from a new machine-
may not reflflect physically realistic operating conditions.
In a newly commissioned tokamak, it is unlikely that
only disrupted shots would be produced. Nonetheless,
we have included these cases for two main reasons. First,
their inclusion is consistent with prior literature (all cases
are available in [58]). Second, there is a machine learning
rationale: for example, when designing a model for anomaly
detection rather than binary classifification, a dataset that
underrepresents disruptions may be advantageous.
Implementation Details
The DisruptionBench framework is implemented in object-
oriented design. DisruptionBench is a class that
accepts four hyperparameters (all of which are thresholds
that we denote with T), the outputted “disruptivity” scores,
and the timebase of the output. Disruptivity is defifined as the
probability of the discharge ending in a disruption sometime
in the future, i.e. p(d X 1∶t ) , where p is defifined per timestep t,
26 Page 6 of 29 Journal of Fusion Energy (2025) 44:26
d is a disruption and X 1∶t are all observed covariates through
the timestep t for which p is expressed. In order, the four
thresholds are defifined as:
1. T high: the higher of two disruptivity thresholds. When
predicted disruptivity is above T high, we increase a
counter that leads to classifification of a disruption. The
value is a flfloat in the range 0-1.
2. T low: the lower of two disruptivity thresholds. When
predicted disruptivity drops below this threshold, we
reset the counter. The value is a flfloat in the range 0-1.
3. T hyst: an integer time step threshold that defifines the
counter mentioned in the defifinition of T high.
4. T useful: an integer time step threshold that defifines how
many steps are necessary for a predicted outcome to be
useful to a system (also referred as mitigation time).
In temporal order, we now describe exactly how the
algorithm simulates a DMS. First, the algorithm monitors
the predicted disruptivity scores to see if they exceed T high
threshold, in which case a counter is increased per step.
Second, while the counter is increasing but still below T hyst,
the disruptivity may fall considerably. If the disruptivity
predictions fall between T high and T low, the counter enters a
static state for as long as the disruptivity stays in that band.
If the disruptivity falls below a second threshold, T low, the
counter is reset. In physical terms, this may occur if the
prediction model detected the emergency of an instability
that then abated suffiffifficiently to be considered back in a safe
region. If, however, the disruptivity stays above T high and
the counter exceeds the value set for T hyst, then the shot is
classifified as a disruption and an “alarm” is triggered. For
model evaluation purposes, we count this as a positive
label by the machine. Please see Fig. 1 for an illustration.
We note that our method reduces to a simple binary
classifification warning cut-offff if T high = T low and T hyst is set
to 1. For a visualization of this evaluation task, please see
Fig. 1.
We defifine true and false positives, and true and false
negatives, according to appropriate predictions in their
relationship to the warning system. For disruptive dis-
charges, if an alarm is triggered before T useful, it is clas-
sifified as a true positive. If not, it is a false negative. For
non disruptive discharges, if an alarm is ever triggered, it
is recorded as a false positive. Else, it is a true negative.
Please see Fig. 2 for an illustration of the above.
A fifinal parameter, T useful, exists to demarcate special
cases during period of time before the end of the discharge
when the DMS no longer has time to intervene to mitigate
a disruption. If a disruption predictor returns a positive to
a disruptive discharge during the time period T useful before
the end, it will still count as a false negative, as the DMS
did not have time to react.

Machine‑Specifific Versus Test‑Case‑Specifific Data
Standardization
In modeling, it is common to scale data either by
normalizing it to have a mean of 0 or by standardizing
it so that its values fall between -1 and 1. Zhu et al. use
machine-specifific scaling parameters to normalize data
across difffferent test cases. Specififically, when standardizing
a feature, they calculate the mean and standard deviation
using the entire dataset from that machine. In few or many
shot cases, this method ensures that the calculated feature
means accurately represent future values.
However, in zero-shot transfer scenarios, using the full
dataset inadvertently exposes information that the model
would not have access to during real-time operation. To
address this, we dynamically compute scaling parameters
using only the training data. As a result, we sometimes
scale unseen test data into ranges that may not physically
characterize the new machine but more accurately reflflect
the conditions of zero-shot performance in actual tokamak
operations.

Model Description
Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are a foundational
architecture in machine learning, particularly for tasks
involving images, videos, and any data that has a spatial
hierarchy. CNNs leverage the spatial correlation present
in data, applying fifilters (kernels) across input features
to produce feature maps that summarize the presence of
specifific patterns or characteristics at various locations
in the input. For readers unfamiliar with the mechanics
of CNNs, we refer them to ref. [67]. For code associated
with this model, please see: https://github.com/Aphoh/
fusion-dp.
Continuous CNNs are a variation of the CNN that
learns the parameters of a continuous function in order to
create a continuous fifilter space which it then discretizes to
use in the conventional CNN machinery. The continuous

Appendix A: A Brief overview of magnetic
fusion tokamaks
Tokamaks [80], one type of toroidal magnetic devices, have
emerged as a major direction of interest within the nuclear
fusion community [81, 82]. In contrast to other leading
approaches (e.g. laser-based inertial confinement fusion
[83]), tokamaks have the capacity for continuous, steady-state
fusion production [84], producing on-demand energy with-
out signifificant land demands or waste. Thus, most of the US
fusion research budget has been dedicated to tokamaks [85].
However, despite their promise, the plasma discharges
in tokamaks currently suffffer from plasma disruptions, or
loss of plasma stability. Indeed, disruptions pose one of
the largest challenges for future commercialization. First,
they are damaging to the device: disruptions deposit large
amounts of heat and stress loads on the plasma facing
components [20], substantially reducing the lifespan of the
device. Second, they have a heterogeneity of causes [3].
Finally, their occurrence halts the discharge, preventing
longer-term energy generation. For more background on
nuclear fusion tokamaks, please see [86, 87].
However, these limitations suggest that probabilistic
modeling approaches might have more success than
simulations in disruption prediction. Indeed, Machine
Learning (ML) models have already been incorporated
into the operations of major tokamaks, including DIII-D
[43], JET [44], and EAST [88]. These models are designed
to perform advanced disruption prediction, or predicting
the occurrence of a plasma disruption while a discharge
is ongoing. Advanced disruption prediction, henceforth
“disruption prediction,” gives the tokamak’s control
systems time to take mitigating steps to limit damage. For
example, one common mitigation approach is to inject noble
gases like Neon or Argon [55], which reduce thermal loads
and induce a “safer” disruption. Another approach is to fifire
a heavy pellet of frozen hydrogen into the center of the
plasma, stopping the discharge [73]. However, numerous
challenges to ML-based disruption prediction models still
exist, as we discuss in Sect. 2.

Appendix F.1.1: Encoder: Embeddings Description
In the context of
ML, embeddings are dense vector representations of
data in which similar data points are close to each other
in the embedding space. The encoding of embeddings is
important when the original text themselves are highly
dimensional and diffiffifficult to use directly. Text embeddings
are representations of subwords (i.e. groups of letters),
words, phrases, or even entire documents as vectors in a
high-dimensional space. They “embed” text from a much
larger input space (in the case of word-level inputs, a
vocabulary can be
) to a smaller “hidden” space
(typically chosen to be O(100) dimensions). These
embeddings capture semantic information in a spatial
representation, meaning that inputs with similar meanings
are represented by vectors that are close to each other in
the embedding space.
Text embeddings are typically obtained in two ways: (1)
Pre-trained Embeddings: Vectors obtained from models
trained on large text corpora, such as Word2Vec [93],
GloVe [94], or embeddings from models like BERT [95]
or GPT. These embeddings are learned in an unsupervised
manner and can capture a wide range of linguistic
properties. (2) Learned Embeddings: Vectors learned
in the context of a supervised task (e.g., classifification,
translation) that a model is trained on. These embeddings
are task-specifific and can adapt to the nuances of the text
relevant to the task. They are a form of end-to-end learning
The underlying mechanisms of transformer models (i.e.
self-attention, positional embeddings, and position-wise
feed-forward layers) are not inherently limited to textual
data. Transformers operate on sequences of vectors, making
no assumptions about the nature of the vectors themselves.
This property enables the application of transformers to non-
textual data, provided that the data can be represented as
sequences of vectors, or “embeddings." For non-text data,
such as time series, images (when treated as sequences of
pixel data or patches), or any numerical data that can be
ordered sequentially, the concept of embeddings can be
extended. In these cases, embeddings can be thought of as
dense, learned representations of the non-text elements of
the data.
We feed our non-text data directly into the GPT-2,
concatenated into an embedding-like vector. Each time step
is represented as a vector in the same high-dimensional
space. Since generally transformers operate on sequences of
vectors, they are well suited to process these “embeddings"
to learn dependencies and relationships, regardless of
whether original data was textual or numerical. Thus, it
is natural for us to skip the encoding of embeddings and
operate only with the transformer’s decoding architecture.

and relationships encapsulated by the continuous Gabor
space, allowing the CNN to perform feature extraction
and pattern recognition while sensitive to the spatial
hierarchies and dependencies inherent in the original
data.
By adopting this methodology, the framework implemented
by Knigge et al. [70]. bridges a gap between the
mathematical niceties of continuous functions and practical
fruits of over a decade of work in CNNs.
